open_obligations: Note Burns et al.'s own disanalogies (imitation saliency, pretraining leakage).
Check whether weak model errors resemble non-expert human errors.
Do not equate PGR with sandwiching success.
in.other_title: Weak-to-strong learning problem and weak supervisor / strong student setup
in.rationale: Bowman et al. describe sandwiching: non-experts try to align a model more capable than them but less capable than experts, who evaluate the result. Burns et al. replace the weak human with a weak model whose labels train a strong model, calling the strong student's resulting performance the weak-to-strong performance; one uses human non-experts and experts, the other only models, so findings from one should not be read as results for the other.
in.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: how to study supervision of models more capable than the supervisor with current models

open_obligations: Check that Bowman et al.'s sandwiching compares non-expert performance with expert performance in a way comparable to Michael et al.'s judge accuracy
Note that Michael et al.'s 'experts' are human debaters with passage access, not a capable but misaligned model

Note the role difference: in Bowman et al., non-expert participants try to train or align the model and the experts take part only at the end of each experimental cycle to evaluate; in Michael et al., judges are assessed on whether they can perform close to expert level on the basis of the debate, and the experts are the human debaters.
in.other_title: Michael et al. adapt Bowman et al.'s sandwiching design, using human debaters as the experts
in.rationale: The passage names Bowman et al.'s implementation of sandwiching and states the change (human debaters as the experts), so EXTENDS fits.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Sandwiching-style evaluation of scalable oversight; this variant uses expert human debaters in place of an AI model

open_obligations: Check that the authors' judge models really sit below the agents in capability, as sandwiching requires
Confirm Bowman et al.'s simplified setting also used fixed ground-truth labels instead of experts
in.other_title: Kenton et al. adapt Bowman et al.'s simplified sandwiching, replacing weak human groups with LLM judges
in.rationale: Bowman et al. define sandwiching and run a simplified version with ground-truth labels; the authors explicitly adopt that simplification and state their change (LLM judges in place of humans), which is an extension of the evaluation framework.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Use of the sandwiching paradigm with ground-truth labels in place of experts, under LLM rather than human non-experts; in the sandwiching definition non-experts attempt to train or align the model across experimental cycles, whereas here weak LLMs judge stronger LLMs under protocols such as open consultancy

text: The authors describe sandwiching as choosing problem settings where a model is more capable than a typical human but less capable than an expert; non-expert participants then try to train or align the model to do the task reliably without any help or input from experts (including preexisting written materials), and experts take part only at the end of each cycle to evaluate how far the non-experts succeeded.
title: Sandwiching experimental design (Cotra 2021): non-experts align a model, experts evaluate
